_about: The chunk tree of the deep-time Time Machine (CWVault/claude/Plan-Deep-Time.md; the ruling of 6 Oct 2026: six chunks, cut where the evidence changes kind). Times are millions of years ago (ma); 'from' is the older end. Every bar carries 'knownFrom', one line saying what that stretch is known from — the fog line's words. 'colour' is Hazen's colour for that earth. 'marks' are SKETCHES for the bench, from Michael's notes of 5 Oct: the store (stories/timeline-events.json) is the home of events and Stage 6 moves them there with their tails; a 'tail' is the age the thing probably began by, older than the oldest evidence. 'line' names the Time Machine viewing that takes over at the bottom rung.
name: Earth
knownFrom: everything below, each stretch from what survived of it

chunks.name: Making a planet
chunks.knownFrom: a few zircon grains, some moon rocks and meteorites; nothing else survived

marks.label: A cloud lights up
marks.text: Dust and gas collapse and the sun lights. The dust holds about a dozen kinds of mineral: the whole mineral kingdom to start with.

marks.label: Gathering
marks.text: Grains to pebbles to planetesimals to a planet in a few tens of millions of years, hot enough to melt. Iron sinks to the centre, which is why there is a core and a magnetic field.

marks.label: The big thwack
marks.text: A body the size of Mars hits. The splash becomes the moon, fifteen times closer than now, filling a huge piece of the sky, and the day is five or six hours long.

marks.label: Black Earth
marks.text: The magma ocean skins over with basalt. Volcanoes breathe out steam, carbon dioxide and nitrogen: the first air.

marks.label: Blue Earth
marks.text: Cool enough for the steam to fall and stay. The evidence for all of this is a few zircon grains, some moon rocks and meteorites, so this is the thickest fog on the whole bar.

chunks.name: Rock, water, first life
chunks.knownFrom: the oldest surviving rock, four billion years old, and the moon's craters

marks.label: Gray Earth
marks.text: Basalt melts and remelts into granite, which floats, and the first land sticks up out of a world ocean. The oldest surviving rock is 4.0 billion years old; granite was probably forming well before.

marks.label: The oceans nearly lost
marks.text: The late bombardment, read off the moon's craters: hits big enough to boil an ocean, maybe more than once. Even this is argued over.

marks.label: Life, probably
marks.text: Carbon in rocks at 3.8 billion that looks like life's leftovers, disputed. Layered mounds built by microbes at 3.5 billion, not disputed.

chunks.name: The rusting of the world
chunks.knownFrom: rocks that record the air and the sea: iron that stayed dissolved, then iron that fell as rust

chunks.name: The long wait
chunks.knownFrom: rock and iron that show no oxygen yet, and the first big continents

marks.label: Water split
marks.text: Cyanobacteria learn to split water for its hydrogen and throw the oxygen away. Nobody agrees when. Then nothing shows for hundreds of millions of years, because iron in the sea, volcanic gas and rock eat the oxygen as fast as it is made.

marks.label: Kenorland
marks.text: The first big continent assembles. The day is about eighteen hours.

chunks.name: The rusting
chunks.knownFrom: banded iron and red beds: rock that records oxygen arriving

marks.label: Oxygen in the air
marks.text: The iron in the oceans runs out, oxygen reaches the air, and it destroys the methane that kept the planet warm. Earth freezes, probably for the first time.

marks.label: Banded iron
marks.text: The iron in the sea falls as rust in layers: most of the world's iron ore, including the iron in a bicycle. The places are findable now: Hamersley, Minnesota, Michigan.

marks.label: Red rocks
marks.text: Red rocks on land. The world rusts in the open. Oxygen makes about two thirds of all mineral kinds; the count jumps past four thousand.

chunks.name: The Boring Billion
chunks.knownFrom: a few fossils of single cells, and rocks that say little changed

marks.label: A cell with a nucleus
marks.text: The first fossil you can confidently call a cell with a nucleus. Somewhere in here a cell swallowed a bacterium and kept it: every animal still runs on it.

marks.label: Bangiomorpha
marks.text: A red seaweed: the oldest fossil with clear sexes and a body of many cells. The important inventions were made in the boring part.

marks.label: Rodinia breaks
marks.text: The supercontinent splits, new coasts weather fast, oxygen begins to climb. The end of boredom.

chunks.name: The end of boredom
chunks.knownFrom: glacial rubble in rocks that sat at the equator, then the first fossils of bodies

chunks.name: Rodinia and the snowballs
chunks.knownFrom: glacial rubble in rocks that were at the equator, and the limestone laid on top of it

marks.label: Snowball one
marks.text: Ice reaches the equator and stays for nearly sixty million years. The best evidence is glacial rubble in rocks that sat at the equator at the time, which is why nobody believed it until the 1990s.

marks.label: The thaw
marks.text: Volcanoes keep breathing carbon dioxide into air that cannot get rid of it under the ice, until the greenhouse wins all at once. Ice to hothouse in a few thousand years.

marks.label: Snowball two
marks.text: Shorter, and the same thaw after it. A smaller one at 580.

chunks.name: The Ediacarans
chunks.knownFrom: the first fossils of bodies, soft ones, kept where volcanic ash buried them

marks.label: Little balls
marks.text: Thousands of tiny fossils in China that look like animal embryos, cells dividing. Or something else. The argument has run thirty years.

marks.label: Fronds in the dark
marks.text: Deep, lightless seafloor covered in fractal fronds with no mouths and no guts, buried by ash where they lived. Charnia was found in a quarry in 1957 by a schoolboy; a girl had found it the year before and was told such rocks have no fossils.

marks.label: Dickinsonia
marks.text: A flat ribbed oval up to a metre long. In 2018 somebody found cholesterol in one, which only animals make, settling a forty-year argument with a smell.

marks.label: Bites and shells
marks.text: The first burrows, so something had a front and a back. The first shells, Cloudina. Holes bored in some of them: the first predators.

chunks.name: The visible world
chunks.knownFrom: fossils hard enough to keep; from 200 million years the seafloor's magnetic stripes; at the end, ice that counts the years

chunks.name: Shells, eyes, and the move to land
chunks.knownFrom: fossils with hard parts, and rock magnetism for how far north the land was, never how far east

chunks.name: The explosion
chunks.knownFrom: the first fossils hard enough to keep, and a few muds that kept the soft parts too

marks.label: Animals, kept
marks.text: Within twenty million years nearly every body plan animals have ever had shows up: eyes, legs, shells, guts, hunters. Shells are life making rock. The oldest shelled fossils are 539; animals were around well before, soft and unfossilised.

marks.label: Chengjiang
marks.text: Chengjiang, and ten million years later the Burgess Shale: whole communities kept in mud, soft parts and all. Anomalocaris, the first big hunter.

marks.label: The map clears
marks.text: The map comes out of the fog. Most of the land is clumped in the south as Gondwana; warm shallow seas flood the rest.

chunks.name: The move to land
chunks.knownFrom: fossils of plants and animals in rock laid down on land

marks.label: Plants ashore
marks.text: Mosses and liverworts on wet rock, turning rock into soil and clay: the mineral count's last rise.

marks.label: A short, sharp ice age
marks.text: It kills most of what lives in the sea. First of the big five dyings.

marks.label: Animals ashore
marks.text: Millipedes, then scorpion-like things, into plants that now have stems. Fish get jaws.

marks.label: A fish with wrists
marks.text: Tiktaalik. Real forests at 385. The first four-legged animals, still mostly in water.

chunks.name: Coal swamps and the Great Dying
chunks.knownFrom: coal, and the rock above it that has almost nothing in it

marks.label: The egg with a shell
marks.text: So animals could finally leave the water for good.

marks.label: Coal
marks.text: Forests nobody could rot yet, so they became coal. Oxygen at 35 percent: dragonflies with two-foot wings, millipedes the length of a car.

marks.label: The Great Dying
marks.text: Pangaea in one piece, then a million years of Siberian volcanoes, and nine in ten species gone. The worst thing that ever happened.

chunks.name: The dinosaurs' world
chunks.knownFrom: fossils, and from 200 million years the seafloor's magnetic stripes, so the map is crisp

marks.label: Dinosaurs
marks.text: Small at first, in a world recovering from the Great Dying.

marks.label: Pangaea splits
marks.text: The seafloor from here on still carries its magnetic stripes, so the map is crisp from now on.

marks.label: Flowers
marks.text: Flowers.

marks.label: The asteroid
marks.text: The asteroid.

chunks.name: Our world
chunks.knownFrom: fossils, then ice cores and sea-floor mud that count the years

chunks.name: The mammals take the empty seats
chunks.knownFrom: fossils, and the seafloor's stripes for where everything was

marks.label: A hot spike
marks.text: Horses the size of dogs.

marks.label: Grasslands
marks.text: Grasslands spread, and with them grazers and the animals that chase them.

marks.label: Walking upright
marks.text: Somewhere in Africa.

chunks.name: The ice ages
chunks.knownFrom: ice cores, sea-floor mud, and the sea's old shorelines

marks.label: The ice comes and goes
marks.text: Every hundred thousand years or so. Sea level rises and falls with it; this is where the sea-level layer earns its keep.

marks.label: Homo sapiens
marks.text: The oldest bones are 300,000 years old; they were 200,000 until a Moroccan site was redated.

marks.label: The last glacial maximum
marks.text: Ice over Chicago and Dublin; sea level 120 metres lower; a land bridge to Alaska.

chunks.name: After the ice
chunks.knownFrom: ice cores by the year, tree rings, and what people wrote

marks.label: The ice lets go
marks.text: The Time Machine's own line starts here.

marks.label: Writing
marks.text: The oldest tablets are from Uruk; writing itself is older, on things that rotted.
